etymology: From the Scots surname Guthrie; a Scottish Covenanter minister, author of The Christian’s Great Interest.
biblical_def: William Guthrie was a Scottish minister of the Covenanting age, pastor of Fenwick in Ayrshire, and the author of one little book of such worth that Owen carried it in his pocket and called the author one able to teach them all. The book, The Christian’s Great Interest, deals with the two great questions of the troubled soul: how a man may know that he has a saving interest in Christ, and how he that lacks it may attain it. Guthrie pressed the apostle’s charge to examine ourselves whether we be in the faith, and prove our own selves (2Co 13:5), and the promise that the things are written that they who believe on the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life (1Jo 5:13). The dictionary honours Guthrie as a wise physician of the conscience and a master of the doctrine of assurance, who would have no man rest in a false peace nor sink in a needless despair, but make his calling and election sure (2Pe 1:10). He taught that as many as receive Christ are given power to become the sons of God (Joh 1:12), and showed the marks by which a soul may try its interest in Him. He was silenced for his nonconformity, and died young; but his one book has guided thousands to a settled assurance founded not on feeling but on Christ received by faith.
webster_summary: A Scottish Covenanter minister whose book The Christian’s Great Interest is a classic on assurance and saving interest in Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Guthrie is his wise dealing with the great question of assurance. He would have no man rest in a false peace nor sink in a needless despair, but examine himself whether he be in the faith, and so come to a settled knowledge of his interest in Christ. The dictionary honours this physician of the conscience, whose one small book has guided thousands.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the doctrine of assurance, the knowledge that a believer may have of his own salvation. Against both the presumption that rests in a false peace and the despair that doubts the grace of God, Guthrie set the Scriptural way: receive Christ by faith, examine the soul by the marks of grace, and make calling and election sure. The assurance he taught is founded not on the changing frames of feeling but on Christ received and the promises believed; and it is the birthright of the children of God, to be sought and not neglected.

etymology: From the surname Welsh; the Scottish minister of Ayr, son-in-law of John Knox and a man of mighty prayer.
biblical_def: John Welsh was a Scottish minister of the early seventeenth century, pastor of Ayr and son-in-law of John Knox, a man so given to prayer that he was said to count the day ill spent that did not see seven or eight hours upon his knees, after the pattern of his Lord, who continued all night in prayer to God (Luk 6:12). He was a faithful preacher who saw his town reformed and many converted. When King James sought to bring the Scottish church under the crown’s control and to silence the free assemblies, Welsh stood for the crown rights of Christ, the Head over all things to the church (Eph 1:22), who is the head of the body and must have in all things the preeminence (Col 1:18). For this he was imprisoned and then banished to France, where he laboured many years, refusing to purchase his return by submission. The dictionary honours Welsh as a man of prayer and a confessor of the sole headship of Christ over His church, who held with the apostles that we must hearken unto God rather than unto men (Act 4:19). His life teaches that the church has but one King and Head, and that her ministers owe their first allegiance to Him, though it cost them home and country.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the sole headship of Christ over His church. The church has but one King, and her ministers owe their first allegiance to Him, hearkening unto God rather than unto men. etymology: From the surname Renwick; the last of the Scottish Covenanter martyrs, executed in 1688.
biblical_def: James Renwick was the last of the Scottish Covenanter martyrs, a young field-preacher of the Killing Times who carried the gospel to the hunted remnant in the moors and hills when the curates had filled the pulpits and the dragoons hunted the faithful. He preached in the open air to gathered conventicles at the peril of his life, baptizing the children of the persecuted and feeding the scattered flock. Taken at last in Edinburgh, he was condemned and hanged in the year sixteen hundred and eighty-eight, the last to die on the scaffold for the Covenant, dying with joy and steadfastness at the age of six and twenty. The dictionary honours Renwick among the noble army of martyrs, who was faithful unto death and received the crown of life (Rev 2:10), and who overcame by the blood of the Lamb and the word of his testimony, loving not his life unto the death (Rev 12:11). He was of those of whom the world was not worthy, who wandered in deserts and in mountains and in dens and caves of the earth (Heb 11:38). For him to live was Christ and to die was gain (Php 1:21). His death closed the long roll of the Covenant’s martyrs, and within months the persecuting house was driven out and liberty came; the blood of the last martyr was as the seed of the church’s deliverance.

The dictionary names this persecution for what it was, and honours the young martyr who met it with joy.

What is honourable in Renwick is his faithfulness unto death in the darkest hour. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the steadfastness of the martyr. He was faithful unto death and received the crown of life; he overcame by the blood of the Lamb and loved not his life unto the death; he was of those of whom the world was not worthy. His death closed the long roll of the Covenant’s martyrs, and within months the persecuting house was cast out and liberty came; so the blood of the last martyr was as the seed of the church’s deliverance.

etymology: From the surname Cargill; a Scottish Covenanter field-preacher and martyr, executed in 1681.
biblical_def: Donald Cargill was a Scottish Covenanter, a bold field-preacher of the Killing Times who would not bow to the crown’s usurpation of the rights of Christ over His church. At the Torwood he solemnly excommunicated the king and his chief persecutors for their tyranny and perjury against the cause of Christ, an act of fearless witness that sealed his own doom. He preached that Christ alone is King in His church, who has on His vesture and on His thigh the name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS (Rev 19:16), and bade the rulers of the earth kiss the Son, lest He be angry and they perish from the way (Psa 2:12). Taken at last, he was hanged at Edinburgh in sixteen hundred and eighty-one, dying with great composure and joy. The dictionary honours Cargill as a faithful confessor and martyr, who held with the apostles that we ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29), and who feared not them which kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Mat 10:28). His witness teaches that the crown of Christ is above the crowns of kings, and that the church owes no earthly sovereign the obedience due to her Lord alone.

etymology: From the surname Cameron; the Scottish Covenanter field-preacher called the Lion of the Covenant, killed at Airds Moss in 1680.
biblical_def: Richard Cameron was a Scottish Covenanter field-preacher of the Killing Times, so bold and fervent in his witness that he was called the Lion of the Covenant. He preached to the gathered remnant in the open moors when to do so was to risk death, and his followers took his name, the Cameronians, a people resolved to maintain the crown rights of Christ against a persecuting state. He fell sword in hand at Airds Moss in sixteen hundred and eighty, refusing to forsake the cause of Christ. The dictionary honours Cameron as a faithful preacher and witness who fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith (2Ti 4:7), and who, faithful unto death, received the crown of life (Rev 2:10). He counted that for him to live was Christ, and to die was gain (Php 1:21), and ran with patience the race set before him, compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1). His brief and burning ministry, and his death in the field, set him among the worthies of the Covenant, and his name became a banner for those who would yield to no earthly power the obedience owed to Christ the King.

etymology: From the surname Peden; a Scottish Covenanter field-preacher of the Killing Times, called Peden the Prophet.
biblical_def: Alexander Peden was a Scottish Covenanter field-preacher of the Killing Times, hunted for years through the moors and hills of the southwest, and so often delivered from his pursuers that the people called him Peden the Prophet. Ejected from his parish for refusing to submit to the crown’s curates, he preached to the scattered remnant in caves and on the open hills, baptizing and comforting the persecuted, ever fleeing from one place to another as the dragoons sought his life. He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty (Psa 91:1); and Peden lived that promise, hidden in the clefts and dens of the earth, going forth unto Christ without the camp, bearing His reproach (Heb 13:13). The Lord’s own word was his rule, that when they persecute you in one city, flee ye into another (Mat 10:23). The dictionary honours Peden as a faithful minister who kept the gospel alive among a hunted people in a dark and bloody time, of whom the world was not worthy (Heb 11:38). His long endurance, his prayers, and his strange deliverances made him a comfort to the suffering remnant, and his life teaches that God hides and keeps His servants in the day of trouble, and that the gospel cannot be silenced though its preachers be driven to the wilderness.

etymology: From the Scots surname Guthrie; a Scottish Covenanter minister, the first to be martyred for the Covenant at the Restoration.
biblical_def: James Guthrie was a Scottish Covenanter minister, a man of small stature but unbending spirit, who stood firmly for the crown rights of Christ over His church and against the supremacy of the king in matters of religion. At the Restoration of Charles the Second, when the crown moved to overthrow the Reformed settlement and bind the church under the royal will, Guthrie would not yield, and in sixteen hundred and sixty-one he was the first minister to die on the scaffold for the cause, hanged at Edinburgh. He held with the apostles that we ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29), and with the three Hebrew children that, come what may, we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up (Dan 3:18). The dictionary honours Guthrie as a faithful confessor and the first martyr of the Restoration persecution, who feared not them which kill the body (Mat 10:28), and who, faithful unto death, received the crown of life (Rev 2:10). His head was set upon the Netherbow of Edinburgh, but his witness could not be silenced; and his steadfastness, that the church owns no head but Christ, lit the long testimony of the Covenant’s martyrs that followed.

Like the three children before the golden image, Guthrie said in effect, be it known, we will not serve thy gods; he obeyed God rather than men and feared not them which kill the body. His head was set upon the Netherbow, but his witness could not be silenced, and his death lit the long testimony of the Covenant’s martyrs that followed after him.

etymology: From the surname Bonar; a nineteenth-century Free Church of Scotland minister, brother of Horatius Bonar and biographer of Robert Murray M’Cheyne.
biblical_def: Andrew Bonar was a minister of the Free Church of Scotland in the nineteenth century, brother of the hymn-writer Horatius Bonar, and one of the most saintly men of his age. He is best remembered as the biographer of his friend Robert Murray M’Cheyne, whose Memoir and Remains, gathered by Bonar, has stirred more men to holiness and to the love of Christ than almost any book of its kind. Bonar himself was a man of deep prayer and Christ-filled devotion, whose diary breathes a continual longing after God and a tender walk with the Saviour. His Commentary on Leviticus opened to many the gospel hidden in the sacrifices, that it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul (Lev 17:11). The dictionary honours Bonar as a pastor of rare holiness who followed peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord (Heb 12:14), and whose one desire was that of Paul, that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings (Php 3:10). He walked in the light as God is in the light, knowing that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth from all sin (1Jo 1:7). His life and his pen alike pressed upon the church the pursuit of holiness and the nearness of the believing soul to Christ.

In an age of growing coldness and busy religion, he kept a near and tender walk with the Saviour, and his Memoir of M’Cheyne and his own diary have stirred countless souls to follow after holiness. The dictionary honours this pastor of prayer, whose one desire was to know Christ and the power of His resurrection.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the pursuit of holiness and the nearness of the believing soul to Christ. Bonar opened in Leviticus the gospel of the atoning blood, for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul, and pressed upon the church that we follow holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. He walked in the light as God is in the light, resting in the blood of Jesus that cleanseth from all sin. His life rebukes a religion content with orthodoxy without communion, and calls the saints to know Christ and to be made conformable unto His death.

etymology: From the surname Berridge; an eighteenth-century evangelical vicar of Everton and awakening preacher of the gospel of free grace.
biblical_def: John Berridge was an eighteenth-century evangelical minister, vicar of Everton in Bedfordshire, who for many years preached a barren religion of works until he was brought, late in life, to the gospel of free grace, and thenceforth preached Christ and the new birth with such power that revival broke out under his ministry. He became a tireless itinerant, riding far and wide to preach to thousands in fields and barns, a friend and fellow-labourer of Whitefield and the Wesleys in the great awakening. He had learned in his own soul the necessity of the new birth, and pressed upon all the Lord’s word, Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again (Joh 3:7). He set before sinners the simple way of salvation, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved (Act 16:31), assuring them that by grace are they saved through faith, not of themselves, the gift of God (Eph 2:8). The dictionary honours Berridge as an awakening preacher of free grace, who knew that if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2Co 5:17). His own late conversion from legal religion to the gospel teaches that a man may preach long without knowing the grace he names, and that the power of an awakening ministry lies in the free grace of God laid hold of in the preacher’s own heart.

corruption_summary: He was brought from a religion of works to the gospel of free grace, and preached the new birth with awakening power.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Berridge first preached, and then was delivered from, was the religion of works, the legal striving that knows nothing of free grace and the new birth. For years he laboured under it, and his ministry was barren; but when he was brought to the gospel of grace, the same pulpit became a fountain of life, and revival followed. The dictionary marks this turning as a witness against the legalism that may lurk even in a preacher’s own heart.

What is honourable in Berridge is the awakening power of his gospel once he had found it. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the power of an awakening ministry lies in the free grace of God laid hold of in the preacher’s own soul. He had learned that a man must be born again, and that salvation is by grace through faith, not of works; and preaching what he now knew in himself, he saw multitudes converted. His late deliverance teaches that a man may preach long without the grace he names, and that the new birth must be a preacher’s own before it is his message.

etymology: From the surname Gadsby; an early-nineteenth-century Strict and Particular Baptist preacher of Manchester and compiler of a famous hymn-book.
biblical_def: William Gadsby was an early-nineteenth-century Strict and Particular Baptist preacher of Manchester, risen from poverty and little schooling to become one of the most beloved preachers of free and sovereign grace in the north of England. He preached the gospel of the electing love of God and the finished work of Christ with great plainness and power to crowds of common people, and he was a tender friend of the poor, labouring for their relief as well as their souls. He compiled a hymn-book, long known as Gadsby’s Hymns, which gathered the richest hymns of free grace and is sung among the Particular Baptists to this day. The dictionary honours Gadsby as a faithful herald of sovereign grace, who held with the apostle that if by grace, then is it no more of works, otherwise grace is no more grace (Rom 11:6), and that men are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:24). He preached salvation by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:9), and saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy (Tit 3:5). His plain preaching and his hymn-book together carried the gospel of free grace to the poor, and taught a people to sing the praises of the God who saves without money and without price.

corruption_summary: He preached free and sovereign grace to the poor, that salvation is of grace and not of works, lest any should boast.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Gadsby preached against was every mingling of works with grace, the proud notion that man contributes something to his own salvation. He held the pure doctrine of free and sovereign grace, that if salvation be by grace it is no more of works, and that men are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ. The dictionary honours this plain and powerful preaching of grace to the common people.

What is honourable in Gadsby is his preaching of free grace to the poor and his gathering of the hymns by which they might sing it. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is salvation by grace alone, not of works, lest any man should boast. He saved us, says the apostle, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy; and Gadsby pressed this home to crowds who had nothing to bring, that they might rest wholly on the mercy of God. His hymn-book taught a people to sing the praises of the God who saves without money and without price.
